entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Felix III, who served as the Bishop of Rome from March 13, 483, until his death on March 1, 492, stands as a pivotal figure in the burgeoning schism between the Western and Eastern Churches. His pontificate was defined by an uncompromising defense of Nicene orthodoxy against the Henotikon, an imperial decree issued by Emperor Zeno in 482, which sought to reconcile Monophysites with Chalcedonians through deliberate ambiguity. Felix III's resolute stance against this theological compromise, which he viewed as an illicit imperial intrusion into doctrinal matters, ignited the Acacian Schism, a significant rupture that would last for 35 years and profoundly shaped the future dynamics of papal authority and Byzantine relations.

The core of Felix III's actions centered on his repudiation of the Henotikon and the subsequent excommunication of Acacius, the Patriarch of Constantinople. In 484, Felix convened a synod in Rome that condemned the Henotikon as heretical and formally anathematized Acacius, along with his supporters, for endorsing the imperial edict and for removing the name of Pope Simplicius from the diptychs. This bold assertion of Roman primacy, extending to the right to judge and condemn an Eastern patriarch, marked a critical escalation in the East-West ecclesiastical tensions, moving beyond mere theological disagreement to a direct challenge of authority and jurisdiction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Felix III's papacy was regionally significant for initiating the Acacian Schism, which lasted 35 years and created a deep ecclesiastical divide between Rome and Constantinople. His actions solidified the papacy's assertion of universal jurisdiction and set a precedent for challenging imperial interference in doctrinal matters.
